text: Up to now we've talked about these platforms in general terms. This lesson is more practical: how do you actually read each vendor's official documentation, as a developer, without getting lost in content meant for a DBA?

Bookmark these four sites now. Microsoft's docs live at learn-dot-microsoft-dot-com. Oracle's at docs-dot-oracle-dot-com. MySQL's at dev-dot-mysql-dot-com-slash-doc. And PostgreSQL's at postgresql-dot-org-slash-docs. These are always more current and more authoritative than any blog post, including this course.

Every vendor describes its SQL commands with syntax diagrams. The notation varies slightly, but the idea is universal: uppercase words are literal keywords, lowercase words are placeholders, square brackets mean optional, and curly braces mean choose exactly one. As a developer, focus on the diagram and the examples below it.

Watch specifically for callouts that say whether a feature is part of the standard or a vendor-specific extension. PostgreSQL's documentation is especially good about flagging this. It tells you directly whether what you just learned will carry over to another platform -- which is exactly the skill this whole course is built around.

And always check which version a doc page describes. Oracle's identity column syntax, for example, built on sequences under the hood, was only added in Oracle twelve c -- it simply doesn't exist in older versions you might still be supporting at work.
Next lesson, we put all of this together: the exact same query, written correctly in five different dialects, side by side. See you there.
